How to find the link in a Connections puzzle

A word can have more than one meaning. Here’s how to spot the connection that fits every clue.

By Biel Sardà · Published 23 Sept 2026 · Suggest a correction

Start with the first connection you notice

To solve a Connections puzzle, look for one relationship that fits every clue. Try a meaning, a sound or a shared category, then check the whole set. A link that fits only some clues needs another look.

Bark, trunk, leaf, root. You probably thought of a tree before reaching the end of the list. Yet bark can also be a dog’s sound, a trunk can hold luggage, and a root can be part of a plant.

That is what makes a connections puzzle interesting: several meanings may be possible, but one relationship brings the clues together. Your first thought is a good place to start. Check it against the rest of the set before choosing.

The dictionary lists both the tree covering and the dog sound under bark. The clue stays the same; the meaning you choose changes.

Find a link you can explain

“Things you find outside” could describe thousands of objects. “Parts of a tree” explains this set much more clearly.

Try finishing a sentence such as “Each clue is a…” or “Each word can follow…”. If the sentence works for every clue, you have a promising answer. If one word needs a different explanation, take another look.

In BrainiLab Connections, you choose the shared relationship from the available answers. Read those choices carefully: games with similar names can have different rules.

Same sound, opposite meanings—or one group?

The same word can give you different kinds of clues. Start by asking what you are comparing.

Three ways words can connect
ExampleWhat connects it?Try the idea
Flour / flowerThey sound alike: a pair of homophones.Choose a word using its sentence
Dust a shelf / dust dough with flourOne word describes removing or adding particles: a contronym.Try the two meanings of dust
Bark / trunk / leaf / rootIn this example, they are all parts of a tree.Say the category, then check each word.

A puzzle does not have to use all three types. The important habit is to explain your proposed link and check every clue, rather than choosing a clever idea that fits only one.

Give the awkward clue another look

Sometimes three words fit straight away and the fourth seems out of place. That awkward word may be the most useful clue. Think of another meaning for it, then see whether the other words fit that meaning too.

What links shift, space and return in a computer context?

They are keyboard keys. Reading the words in that context brings all three together.

Make sense of the answer

If a connection surprises you, go back to the clue that was hardest to place. Was there a meaning you had forgotten, or a category you had not considered?

Understanding that one link gives you something to try in the next round, even when the words are completely different.
